2. One Jadav Chandra Mali who has since died, filed an application under section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (hereinafter referred to) as "The State Acquisition Act") for pre-emption of certain lands which appertained to a holding recorded in Khatian No. 55 of Mouza Shahadebpur. The pre-emptor claimed that the said holding was owned by him and the respondents No. 2 to 5 and that the respondent No.1, who was a stranger, purchased 13 acre of land thereof from respondents No. 2 and 3 by a kabala dated 3-2-1964 without service of any notice upon him. According to the pre-emptor he came to know about the sale for the first time in Falgoon, 1371 B.S. when a temporary but was raised on the land. The purchaser resisted the claim for pre-emption on the ground that the pre-emptor had knowledge of the purchase and that the disputed land was a Chandina land within a Municipal area and therefore section 96 of the State Acquisition Act had no application to the purchase in question. The learned Munsif allowed the application for pre-emption and his decision was affirmed on appeal by a Subordinate Judge. The respondent No.1, the purchaser, thereupon filed an application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the High Court. In the High Court a petition was filed on behalf of the pre-emptor under Order 6, rule 17 read with section 151 and Section 153 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the application for pre-emption whereby the application for pre-emption was sought to be converted to an application under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act but the application was rejected on the ground that it would change the nature of the case. The learned Judges came to the finding that as the land in question was within a Municipal area, section 96 of the State Acquisition Act was wrongly applied by the Courts below and upon this finding made the rule obtained by the respondent No. 1 absolute and set aside the order of the learned Subordinate Judge. Thereafter the heirs of the pre-emptor Jadav Chandra Mali obtained special leave from the Supreme Court of Pakistan for consideration of the following contentions :- 

 1) That the amendment prayed for was of a technical nature and in view of the fact that the relief prayed for in the original application could be given under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and the deposit that was made was in excess of the amount required under the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, the application for amendment should have been allowed. 

 2) That the relief prayed for in the application under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act could be given under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act even if no application for amendment had been made. 

 4. In that case the High Court approved the order rejecting the application for amendment upon the finding that by the amendment the plaintiff sought to "substitute new grounds for the suit". Before we proceed further, we would like to pre-produce sub-section (1) of Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which is as follows:- 

 5. The pre-emptor wanted to, exercise his right of pre-emption in respect of the disputed land on the ground that he was a co-sharer tenant of the tenancy to which the said land appertained. The application was described as one coming under section 96 of the State Acquisition Act. Subsequently when it was realized that having regard to the nature of the disputed land the relief prayed for could be granted under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, an application for amendment to that effect in the cause title of the application with consequential changes was made but the High Court rejected the prayer on the ground inter alia, that the change sought to be made was not "a mere change of one kind of pre-emption to another", but it was "substitution of a new case altogether". Since a co-sharer tenant of non-agricultural and is entitled to apply for pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, it does not appear how the nature and character of the application can be said to be altered by substitution of a new case altogether by reason of the amendment prayed for. Whatever changes were sought to be made were changes in form and not in substance. In the circumstances we find that the learned Judges were not justified in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the application upon the view they took. Moreover, since the relief prayed for could be given by the Court under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, even if that section had not been specifically mentioned in the application, it was not necessary either to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title. 

 6. It appears that unfortunately the attentions of the learned Judges of the High Court in the instant case were not invited to a decision of that Court reported in (1967) 19 DLR 347- P.L.D. 1967 (Dacca) 588 where the learned Judges strongly disapproved of the view taken by an Additional District Judge who allowed appeals and dismissed applications for preemption only on the ground that the applications under section 26-F of the Bengal Tenancy Act were made at a time when the said section was not applicable in the district of Dacca where the lands were situated and it was held that:- 

 “If the relief claimed by the petitioner was allowable under some other law of the country, namely, section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, then the Court of appeal below was bound to apply the same notwithstanding the mis-description of the cause title in the application.”
